role.altitude: The computer science teacher keeps explaining, reviewing students' code, setting grades as examiner, revising courses and helping students in office hours; copying check-off lists, typing autograder scores and re-keying grades into the student system shrink.
skills_to_grow: Writing test suites that grade the right things and keeping the gradebook set up
role.ambitious_version: A teacher who updates a programming course every year from what students struggled with, without losing evenings to admin.

tasks.short: Have lab attendance and check-offs recorded, maintain student attendance records, enter assignment and exam grades, combine final grades, check them as examiner, transfer them to the student system, keep the exam file and handle grade questions.

steps.what: Students sign in at lab sessions
Teaching assistants check off lab assignments that students demonstrate
Computer science teacher maintains student attendance records and check-offs in a spreadsheet from the paper lists
Computer science teacher enters programming assignment and exam grades in the gradebook
Computer science teacher combines component grades into final grades with the course weighting
Computer science teacher checks the final grades and borderline cases as examiner
Computer science teacher types the final grades into the student administration system
Computer science teacher keeps the exam file for the examination board: exam, answer key, grades and analysis
Computer science teacher answers students' grade questions and makes corrections

approvals.approved_version: final grade list as checked and confirmed by the examiner in s6; any later change needs a new check

tasks.design: Students scan the session code in the LMS when they arrive at a lab, and teaching assistants tick demonstrated assignments on a tablet in the LMS instead of a paper list. The autograder runs each assignment's test suite on submission and writes the test score to the gradebook; the teacher enters code review and exam scores. Gradebook formulas apply the course weighting. After the teacher checks the final list as examiner, the university's gradebook link transfers exactly that list to the student administration system, and an export bundles exam, key, grades and item analysis for the exam file. No model sets or changes a grade.
tasks.previous_blocker: Lab lists were on paper, and grades were combined in spreadsheets and typed twice: into the LMS and the student system.
tasks.enabler_now: LMS attendance codes, autograders that write to the gradebook, and gradebook links to student systems.
tasks.still_hard: Borderline cases and grades disputed by students.
tasks.human_edge: Judging whether a student who failed the tests still understood the problem.
tasks.altitude: Much less copying; the examiner's decision does not change.

reach.learn: Whether tablet check-offs are as quick as the paper list.

evidence.claim: At a Dutch university, grades in the LMS must always also be published in the student system, which is double entry.
A Dutch assessment tool auto-marks closed questions and gives item statistics.
Examiners appointed by the examination board set the results.

assumptions: Boundary: from lab sign-in to grades in the student system and the exam file; exam design and marking are separate tasks.

Input contract for s3: session-code scans by students (s1) with about the effort of signing a list, and LMS check-offs by teaching assistants (s2) with about the effort of ticking paper; about 80% of sessions run this way; the rest are typed; s3 is priced at that share.

Input contract for s4: test scores written to the gradebook by the autograder from each submission's test run; about half of assignment points come from tests; code review and exam scores are entered by the teacher; s4 is priced at that share.
Input contract for s7: the gradebook-to-student-system link set up by the university's education IT, about 85% of courses mapped; unmapped courses are typed.
Grade questions and the examiner check keep their full time; student and assistant time are outside the teacher's savings.
unknowns: Whether the course's LMS is linked to the student system.
research_questions: Do grade corrections after publication fall?

already_counted.description: Computer science teacher checks autograder scores for submissions that failed to build or run.
Computer science teacher checks transfer errors reported by the gradebook link.

incremental.description: Computer science teacher sets up gradebook weighting, session codes and the link mapping each course run.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a theory course graded mostly by written exam in a course not linked to the student system; high: a large programming course with autograded assignments and weekly labs.

tasks.short: Keep abreast of developments in the field by reading current literature and preprints, talking with colleagues, registering for and participating in professional conferences and noting what to use in teaching.

steps.what: Computer science teacher reads current literature: new papers, preprints and alert mails

loop.input: The week's papers from the teacher's saved literature searches and preprint alerts on their topics.
loop.output: A weekly digest with two lines per paper and its link, grouped by topic.
loop.check: Every entry must link to a paper that resolves by DOI or preprint id and repeat its title, or it is dropped; the teacher reads the papers they will use.
loop.why_not_simpler: Alerts list titles; the teacher needs to see quickly what each paper adds.

steps.what: Computer science teacher talks with colleagues in seminars and the corridor
Computer science teacher registers for conferences and books travel
Computer science teacher participates in professional conferences and workshops
Computer science teacher notes developments to use in courses or research

tasks.design: The teacher's saved searches and preprint alerts feed a weekly digest made by a bounded step on the university's own model platform, with two lines and a working link per paper. Talking with colleagues, conferences and deciding what to use stay as they are.
tasks.previous_blocker: Alert mails listed titles only, so many papers had to be opened to judge them.
tasks.enabler_now: Literature tools give topic summaries, and university-run model platforms are available to staff.
tasks.still_hard: Judging which new idea will last.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing from a colleague what really works in practice.
tasks.altitude: Little changes; reading is a bit faster.

reach.learn: Which topics teachers flag as new.

evidence.claim: A literature product gives topic summaries and foundational papers.
A Dutch university offers staff its own chat platform (pilot).

assumptions: Boundary: keeping up with the field; using it in courses is a separate task.
Input contract for s1: the teacher's saved searches in the literature databases and preprint alerts; papers outside them are found as today.
Talks, conferences and notes keep their full time.
unknowns: How many papers a week the teacher scans.
research_questions: Does the digest miss papers the teacher later finds important?

already_counted.description: Computer science teacher opens papers whose digest lines look relevant.

incremental.description: Computer science teacher tunes the saved searches.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a teacher who mostly learns at conferences; high: a fast-moving field with many weekly preprints.

tasks.short: Evaluate the course from evaluations and results, discuss changes, plan and revise curricula, course content, materials, programming assignments and methods of instruction, update the course guide and have assessment changes approved.

steps.what: Computer science teacher evaluates the course from student evaluations, assignment results and assistants' feedback

loop.input: The free-text comments from the course evaluation, run on the university's own model platform.
loop.output: Themes in the comments, each with the number of comments and two quoted examples.
loop.check: Every theme must quote comments word for word from the export and count them, or it is dropped; the teacher reads all comments behind any theme they act on.
loop.why_not_simpler: Scores show what students rated; the comments say why.

steps.what: Computer science teacher discusses changes with colleagues and the programme committee
Computer science teacher plans the revised learning objectives, course plan and methods of instruction
Computer science teacher revises course materials: lecture notes, slides, programming assignments and their test suites

loop.input: An existing programming assignment, its reference solution and the change the teacher wants.
loop.output: A draft new variant of the assignment text and extra test cases.
loop.check: The teacher's updated reference solution must pass every drafted test in the autograder, and every test must fail on a known wrong solution, or the test is dropped; the teacher reviews text and tests.
loop.why_not_simpler: Copying last year's assignment invites reused solutions; writing new tests by hand is slow.

steps.what: Computer science teacher updates the course guide: schedule, objectives and assessment
Examination board approves changes to the course's assessment

tasks.design: Evaluation comments are grouped into themes with quoted examples by a bounded step on the university's own model platform, next to assignment results from the gradebook. For programming assignments, a bounded step drafts new variants and extra tests, which are only kept if the teacher's reference solution passes them and a known wrong solution fails. The course guide is generated from the course plan fields and the timetable. Deciding objectives, methods and assessment stays with the teacher, colleagues and the examination board.
tasks.previous_blocker: Evaluation comments were read one by one and new assignment tests written from scratch.
tasks.enabler_now: University-run model platforms and autograders that run drafted tests against reference solutions.
tasks.still_hard: Choosing what to drop from a full course.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing where students get stuck in a topic.

ambition.what: Revise programming assignments every course run instead of every few years.

tasks.altitude: Revision takes less drafting; course decisions stay with people.

reach.learn: Whether new variants cut questions about unclear specifications.

evidence.claim: A Dutch university runs its own chat platform for staff (pilot) and forbids automated grading on it.
Language models can draft programming exercises and test cases that a reference solution can verify.
Drafting course materials is not an AI Act high-risk use; evaluating learning outcomes is.

assumptions: Boundary: from course evaluation to the approved course guide; teaching the course is outside.
Input contract for s1: the evaluation export from the quality office's survey tool and assignment results from the gradebook; comments are processed only on the university's own platform.
Input contract for s5: course plan fields from s3 and the timetable from the scheduling office's system; fallback is editing last year's guide.
About two thirds of material time goes to programming assignments; lecture notes and slides are revised as today.
Discussion and planning keep their full time; board time is outside the teacher's savings.
unknowns: Number of programming assignments revised per run.
research_questions: Do new assignment variants reduce copied solutions?

already_counted.description: Computer science teacher reviews drafted assignment text and tests.
Computer science teacher reads the comments behind themes they act on.

incremental.description: Computer science teacher keeps a known-wrong solution per assignment for the test check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a theory course with few assignments; high: a programming course with many assignments and a large evaluation.

tasks.short: Let students book office hours, maintain regularly scheduled office hours to advise and assist students with code and study choices, answer repeat questions and note agreements.

steps.what: Students ask for an office hours slot or drop in
Computer science teacher arranges office hours appointments by mail
Computer science teacher assists students with their code and assignments in office hours
Computer science teacher advises students on study and career choices
Computer science teacher answers the same course questions by mail outside office hours
Computer science teacher notes agreements made with a student

tasks.design: Students book office hours slots on the teacher's calendar booking page, which replaces the mail back-and-forth. Questions that come up repeatedly are answered once on the course discussion board in the LMS, and the teacher points to it. Helping with code and advising stay face to face; no chatbot answers students.
tasks.previous_blocker: Slots were arranged by mail and the same questions answered many times.
tasks.enabler_now: Calendar booking pages and LMS discussion boards are standard.
tasks.still_hard: Students who need help but do not come.
tasks.human_edge: Spotting that a coding problem is really a confidence problem.

reach.learn: Which students the teacher refers on.

evidence.claim: Calendar booking pages let students pick an open slot themselves.
A student-facing chatbot must tell students it is AI (model knowledge of AI Act art. 50); the design uses none.

assumptions: Boundary: office hours and the questions around them; formal study advice is the study adviser's work.
Input contract for s2: bookings students make on the booking page (s1) with about the effort of an e-mail; drop-ins stay.
Help and advice keep their full time; students' time is outside the teacher's savings.
unknowns: How many students use office hours per week.
research_questions: Do more students come when booking is easy?

incremental.description: Computer science teacher posts answers to repeat questions on the board.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a small course with drop-in hours; high: a large first-year course with many booking mails and repeat questions.
